pos: n. and adj. (the number 14; rendering Hebrew arba asar, Greek dekatessares)
etymology: Old English fēowertīene, four and ten. Matthew built the opening of his Gospel on it.
biblical_def: Matthew's genealogy is arranged by it: “So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David until the carrying away into Babylon are fourteen generations; and from the carrying away into Babylon unto Christ are fourteen generations” (Mat 1:17). Jacob “served thee fourteen years for thy two daughters” (Gen 31:41). Paul went up to Jerusalem “fourteen years after” his first visit (Gal 2:1), and knew a man caught up to the third heaven “above fourteen years ago” (2Co 12:2). Solomon's dedication feast ran “seven days and seven days, even fourteen days” (1Ki 8:65).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fourteen as four and ten; twice seven.
webster_full: FOURTEEN, a. Four and ten; twice seven.
corruption_summary: Matthew's three fourteens are mined for a secret code, when the arrangement is an aid to memory and a statement about David.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew counts three sets of fourteen and says so, and the numerologist takes the invitation and never comes back. The arrangement is deliberate — Matthew omits kings to make it — and its plain purposes are two: a genealogy in three memorable blocks, and a Gospel whose first sentence calls Jesus “the son of David” and whose first structure is built around David's name. That is as far as the text goes. The corruption is to make the number the message, so that the reader is hunting for a cipher while the evangelist is telling him who the child is. Scripture uses fourteen the way it uses every number: to count real things — years of service, days of a feast, years between two visits to Jerusalem.
roots_summary: Hebrew arba asar (H702, H6240), four and ten; Greek dekatessares (G1180), fourteen.
roots_lines: Hebrew arba asar (H702 with H6240) — fourteen; Genesis 31:41, Numbers 29:13, 1 Kings 8:65.
usage: “Fourteen generations” — three times, and the name in the middle of them is David.
“Fourteen years for thy two daughters” — Jacob's wages.
“Fourteen years after I went up again to Jerusalem” — Paul's independence measured in years.

pos: n. and adj. (the number 16; rendering Hebrew shesh esreh)
etymology: Old English sixtīene, six and ten. In Kings it is a reign's length and a king's age at accession.
biblical_def: Three kings of Judah reigned sixteen years, and two of them were good: Jotham, who “did that which was right” (2Ki 15:33), and Ahaz, who did not (2Ki 16:2). Azariah was made king when he “was sixteen years old” (2Ki 14:21; 2Ch 26:1). Jehoash of Israel also reigned sixteen years (2Ki 13:10). The boards of the tabernacle stood in “sixteen sockets” of silver (Exo 26:25). Zilpah bore Jacob “sixteen souls” (Gen 46:18), and Eleazar's house yielded “sixteen chief men” among the priests (1Ch 24:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sixteen as six and ten; consisting of six and ten.
webster_full: SIXTEEN, a. Six and ten; consisting of six and ten.
corruption_summary: A long reign is read as God's approval, and Ahaz reigned exactly as long as Jotham.
corruption_paragraphs: The books of Kings give Jotham and Ahaz the same sixteen years, and the same reckoning of age at accession, and then diverge on the only sentence that matters: one did right in the sight of the LORD and one did not. Ahaz burned his children in the fire, copied an altar from Damascus, and shut the doors of the house of the LORD, and his sixteen years were as long as his father's. Prosperity theology reads length of tenure as a verdict; the chronicler refuses to, and records the years and the verdict in separate sentences so that no one can confuse them.
roots_summary: Hebrew shesh esreh (H8337, H6240), six and ten.
roots_lines: Hebrew shesh esreh (H8337 with H6240) — sixteen; 2 Kings 13:10, 14:21, 15:33, 16:2, Exodus 26:25, Genesis 46:18.
usage: “Sixteen years reigned he in Jerusalem” — said of a good king and a bad one alike.
“Sixteen years old” — Azariah made king by the people.
“Sixteen sockets” — the silver footing of the tabernacle boards.

pos: n. and adj. (the number 17; rendering Hebrew sheva esreh)
etymology: Old English seofontīene, seven and ten. The number brackets the story of Joseph at both ends.
biblical_def: “Joseph, being seventeen years old, was feeding the flock with his brethren” (Gen 37:2) when the story began; and “Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years” (Gen 47:28) after it ended — the years Joseph had with his father before Egypt matched by the years his father had with him in it. Jeremiah bought his cousin's field in Anathoth during the siege and “weighed him the money, even seventeen shekels of silver” (Jer 32:9). Rehoboam “reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem” (1Ki 14:21), and so did Jehoahaz in Samaria (2Ki 13:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines seventeen as seven and ten.
webster_full: SEVENTEEN, a. Seven and ten; consisting of seven and ten.
corruption_summary: Jeremiah's seventeen shekels are read as a curiosity, when they were the price of a prophet's faith in a city about to fall.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 32 is faith with a receipt. The Chaldeans were at the wall, the prophet was in the court of the prison for saying the city would fall, and the LORD told him to buy a field he would never farm — and he did it properly: witnesses, a sealed deed, an open copy, seventeen shekels weighed out. The reason is given in verse 15: “Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.” Modern faith prefers to be unpriced; Jeremiah's cost seventeen shekels and was filed in an earthen vessel to last many days. The prayer that follows — “Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power… there is nothing too hard for thee” — was prayed after the purchase, not before.
roots_summary: Hebrew sheva esreh (H7651, H6240), seven and ten.
roots_lines: Hebrew sheva esreh (H7651 with H6240) — seventeen; Genesis 37:2, 47:28, Jeremiah 32:9, 1 Kings 14:21, 2 Kings 13:1.
usage: “Joseph, being seventeen years old” — the dreamer in the coat.
“Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years” — the years given back.
“Seventeen shekels of silver” — a field bought under siege.

pos: n. and adj. (the number 18; rendering Hebrew shemoneh esreh, Greek deka kai okto)
etymology: Old English eahtatīene, eight and ten. Luke 13 uses it twice in one chapter, for a tower and a woman.
biblical_def: Luke 13 has the number twice. “Those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?” (Luk 13:4); and “a woman which had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years, and was bowed together” (Luk 13:11), whom the Lord calls “a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan hath bound, lo, these eighteen years” (Luk 13:16). Israel “served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years” (Jdg 3:14) and was oppressed by the Ammonites eighteen years (Jdg 10:8). The two brass pillars of the temple were “eighteen cubits high apiece” (1Ki 7:15). Jehoiachin “was eighteen years old when he began to reign” (2Ki 24:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eighteen as eight and ten.
webster_full: EIGHTEEN, a. Eight and ten united.
corruption_summary: Disasters are read as verdicts on their victims, and the Lord asked the crowd whether the eighteen were sinners above all men.
corruption_paragraphs: Every age reads catastrophe as judgment on the people it fell on, and Luke 13:4 is the Lord's answer to the instinct. Eighteen men died under a tower in Siloam; the crowd assumed they had it coming; Christ said no — and then turned the tower on the crowd: “except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.” The disaster was not a verdict on the eighteen; it was a sermon to the living. Twelve verses later the same number is a woman who has been bent double for eighteen years, and the ruler of the synagogue is angry that she was healed on the sabbath. The Lord's word for her condition is not disease but bondage — “whom Satan hath bound” — and His word for the healing is loosed. The men who counted her eighteen years as her problem, and the sabbath as their principle, had the two the wrong way round.
roots_summary: Hebrew shemoneh esreh (H8083, H6240), eight and ten; Greek deka kai okto (G1176, G3638), ten and eight.
roots_lines: Hebrew shemoneh esreh (H8083 with H6240) — eighteen; Judges 3:14, 10:8, 1 Kings 7:15, 2 Kings 24:8.
Greek deka kai okto (G1176, G3638) — eighteen; Luke 13:4, 13:11, 13:16.
usage: “Those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell” — not sinners above all men.
“Whom Satan hath bound, lo, these eighteen years” — bondage named, and loosed on the sabbath.
“Eighteen cubits high apiece” — Jachin and Boaz.

pos: n. and adj. (the number 60; rendering Hebrew shishim; the AV more often says threescore)
etymology: Old English sixtig. The Authorized Version usually writes threescore; the plain word survives in the ages of Genesis 5 and the valuations of Leviticus 27.
biblical_def: The word stands in the ages of the fathers before the flood: “Enoch lived sixty and five years, and begat Methuselah” (Gen 5:21); “all the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty and five years” (Gen 5:23); “all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years: and he died” (Gen 5:27). The Law values a vowed man “from twenty years old even unto sixty years old” at fifty shekels, and above sixty at fifteen (Lev 27:3, 7). At the dedication of the altar the princes brought “the rams sixty, the he goats sixty, the lambs of the first year sixty” (Num 7:88). And among the returning exiles, “The children of Adonikam, six hundred sixty and six” (Ezr 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sixty as six times ten.
corruption_summary: Adonikam's six hundred sixty and six sons are pressed into the beast's number, and the Law's valuation of a man over sixty is read as contempt for age.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 2:13 counts six hundred sixty and six children of Adonikam coming home from Babylon, and the number means what a census means: that many people. Revelation 13:18 gives the same figure to the beast, and the number-hunters have run between the two verses ever since, as if a family of returned exiles were a cipher. Scripture uses numbers as numbers unless it says otherwise, and in Ezra it does not say otherwise. Leviticus 27 gets the opposite mistreatment: a man above sixty is valued at fifteen shekels against fifty in his prime, and the reader concludes that the Law thinks less of the old. The valuation is of labour vowed to the sanctuary, not of persons; the same chapter values a month-old child at five shekels and Scripture commands the young to rise before the hoary head (Lev 19:32). Worth and wage are different columns.
roots_lines: Hebrew shishim (H8346) — sixty; Genesis 5:15–27, Leviticus 27:3, 27:7, Numbers 7:88, Ezra 2:13.
usage: “Nine hundred sixty and nine years: and he died” — the longest life in the record, and its last clause.
“From twenty years old even unto sixty years old” — the Law's working years.
“The children of Adonikam, six hundred sixty and six” — a census, not a cipher.

pos: n. and adj. (the number 13; rendering Hebrew shelosh esreh)
etymology: Old English thrēotīene, three and ten. Scripture attaches no omen to it; superstition does.
biblical_def: “Ishmael his son was thirteen years old, when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin” (Gen 17:25). Solomon spent seven years on the house of the LORD and “was building his own house thirteen years” (1Ki 7:1). On the first day of the feast of tabernacles Israel offered “thirteen young bullocks” (Num 29:13). The Kohathite priests received “thirteen cities” by lot (Jos 21:4), and Simeon's inheritance closed with “thirteen cities and their villages” (Jos 19:6). The firstborn to be redeemed above the Levites numbered “two hundred and threescore and thirteen” (Num 3:46).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thirteen as ten and three.
webster_full: THIRTEEN, a. Ten and three; as thirteen ounces or pounds.
corruption_summary: Thirteen is feared as unlucky, and the one thing Scripture does with it is count.
corruption_paragraphs: No number in the Bible carries a curse, and the fear of thirteen is a superstition Scripture never heard of. What the text does with the number is arithmetic: the age of Ishmael at his circumcision, the years of Solomon's palace, the bullocks of the first day of the feast. The only edge the number has is one the reader supplies from 1 Kings 6:38 and 7:1 set side by side — seven years for the LORD's house, thirteen for the king's own — and that is not an omen but a proportion, and one every man can check in his own diary. Fearing a number is a form of idolatry, since it credits the number with a power that belongs to God alone; the Christian who will not sit thirteen at a table has given the table a theology.
roots_summary: Hebrew shelosh esreh (H7969, H6240), three and ten.
roots_lines: Hebrew shelosh esreh (H7969 with H6240) — thirteen; Genesis 17:25, 1 Kings 7:1, Numbers 29:13–14, Joshua 19:6, 21:4.
usage: “Ishmael his son was thirteen years old” — circumcised the same day as Abraham.
“Building his own house thirteen years” — against seven for the LORD's.
“Thirteen young bullocks” — the first day of tabernacles.

pos: adj. (the ordinal of eleven; rendering Hebrew ashte asar, Greek hendekatos)
etymology: Old English endleofta. The eleventh hour, from the parable of the labourers, has passed into the language as the last possible moment.
biblical_def: The householder went out “about the eleventh hour” and found others standing idle (Mat 20:6), and “when they came that were hired about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny” (Mat 20:9). Jerusalem “was besieged unto the eleventh year of king Zedekiah” (2Ki 25:2), and Jeremiah's word ran “unto the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah… unto the carrying away of Jerusalem captive in the fifth month” (Jer 1:3). Moses spoke Deuteronomy “in the fortieth year, in the eleventh month” (Deu 1:3). Solomon's house was finished “in the eleventh year, in the month Bul” (1Ki 6:38). The eleventh foundation of the city is “a jacinth” (Rev 21:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eleventh as the next in order to the tenth; the ordinal of eleven.
webster_full: ELEVENTH, a. The next in order to the tenth; the ordinal of eleven.
corruption_summary: The eleventh hour is turned into a licence to delay, and the parable is about the householder's right to be generous, not the labourer's right to be late.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet at the eleventh hour. The first is the murmurers' — that the men who came last should not receive a whole penny, which is the objection of every religion of merit to grace, and the householder's answer stands over all of it: “Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” The second is the modern one — that since the eleventh-hour men were paid in full, a man may plan to come at the eleventh hour. The parable gives no such man. The late labourers had stood idle all day because “no man hath hired us”; they went the moment they were called. The thief on the cross is the eleventh hour; the man who says he will repent later is not planning an eleventh hour but a twelfth, and Scripture records no wages paid at the twelfth.
roots_summary: Hebrew ashte asar (H6249, H6240), eleven, eleventh; Greek hendekatos (G1734), eleventh.
roots_lines: Hebrew ashte asar (H6249 with H6240) — eleventh; Deuteronomy 1:3, 1 Kings 6:38, 2 Kings 25:2, Jeremiah 1:3.
usage: “About the eleventh hour he went out” — grace to men who had waited all day.
“Unto the eleventh year of king Zedekiah” — the siege dated to its end.
“The eleventh, a jacinth” — a foundation of the city.

pos: adj. (the ordinal of twelve; rendering Hebrew shenem asar, Greek dodekatos)
etymology: Old English twelfta. In Esther it is the month of Adar, the month Haman's lot fell on.
biblical_def: Haman's lot “fell” on “the twelfth month, that is, the month Adar” (Est 3:7), and on the thirteenth day of that month, “when the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them… it was turned to the contrary” (Est 9:1). Josiah, “in the twelfth year” of his reign, “began to purge Judah and Jerusalem from the high places” (2Ch 34:3). Jehoiachin was lifted out of prison “in the twelfth month” of the thirty-seventh year of his captivity (2Ki 25:27). Word of Jerusalem's fall reached Ezekiel “in the twelfth year of our captivity” (Eze 33:21). Elisha was found plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, “and he with the twelfth” (1Ki 19:19). The twelfth foundation of the city is “an amethyst” (Rev 21:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines twelfth as the second after the tenth; the ordinal of twelve.
webster_full: TWELFTH, a. The second after the tenth; the ordinal of twelve.
corruption_summary: Haman's lot is read as chance, when the month it chose became the month of Purim.
corruption_paragraphs: Esther 3:7 shows a pagan casting lots for a month to destroy the Jews, and the lot falls on Adar, the twelfth — nearly a year away. The delay is the whole story: it left time for Esther, for the fast, for the king's sleepless night, and for a decree of self-defence, so that on the day Haman's lot had chosen “it was turned to the contrary.” Proverbs 16:33 had already explained the mechanism: “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.” The modern reader calls the timing luck. The book of Esther never names God once, and never lets the reader believe in luck for a single chapter.
roots_summary: Hebrew shenem asar (H8147, H6240), twelve, twelfth; Greek dodekatos (G1428), twelfth.
roots_lines: Hebrew shenem asar (H8147 with H6240) — twelfth; Esther 3:7, 9:1, 2 Chronicles 34:3, 2 Kings 25:27, Ezekiel 33:21.
usage: “The twelfth month, that is, the month Adar” — Haman's lot, and Purim's date.
“In the twelfth year he began to purge Judah” — Josiah at twenty.
“The twelfth, an amethyst” — the last foundation stone.

pos: adj. (the ordinal of thirteen; rendering Hebrew shelosh esreh)
etymology: Old English thrēotēotha. In Jeremiah it dates a prophet's call; in Esther, a day appointed for slaughter that became a day of deliverance.
biblical_def: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah “in the thirteenth year” of Josiah's reign (Jer 1:2), and Jeremiah later counted from it: “From the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon king of Judah, even unto this day, that is the three and twentieth year, the word of the LORD hath come unto me, and I have spoken unto you, rising early and speaking; but ye have not hearkened” (Jer 25:3). Haman's letters appointed “the thirteenth day of the twelfth month” for the destruction of the Jews (Est 3:13), and on that day the Jews gathered themselves “to lay hand on such as sought their hurt” (Est 9:1). The kings of the east “served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled” (Gen 14:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thirteenth as the third after the tenth; the ordinal of thirteen.
webster_full: THIRTEENTH, a. The third after the tenth; the ordinal of thirteen.
corruption_summary: Faithfulness is measured by response, and Jeremiah measured twenty-three years of preaching by the date he began and the fact that no one listened.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 25:3 is the ministry review modern religion cannot bear to read. From the thirteenth year of Josiah to the fourth of Jehoiakim — twenty-three years — the prophet rose early and spoke, “but ye have not hearkened.” He counts the years exactly and reports the result exactly, and he does not conclude that he should have changed the message. The corruption is to make results the measure of a call; Jeremiah was measured by whether he spoke what he was given, and the audience's twenty-three years of not hearing were charged to the audience. A man who dates his calling can also date his faithfulness, and neither date depends on the hearers.
roots_lines: Hebrew shelosh esreh (H7969 with H6240) — thirteenth; Genesis 14:4, Esther 3:12–13, 9:1, Jeremiah 1:2, 25:3.
usage: “From the thirteenth year of Josiah… but ye have not hearkened” — a ministry dated and reviewed.
“The thirteenth day of the twelfth month” — Haman's date, kept by Purim.
“In the thirteenth year they rebelled” — the war that took Lot captive.

pos: adj. (the ordinal of fifteen; rendering Hebrew chamesh esreh, Greek pentekaidekatos)
etymology: Old English fīftēotha. The fifteenth day of the first month is unleavened bread; of the seventh, tabernacles; of the eighth, Jeroboam's invention.
biblical_def: Two of the LORD's feasts fall on it: “on the fifteenth day of the same month is the feast of unleavened bread unto the LORD” (Lev 23:6), and “The fifteenth day of this seventh month shall be the feast of tabernacles” (Lev 23:34). Israel left Rameses “on the fifteenth day of the first month; on the morrow after the passover” (Num 33:3). Jeroboam “ordained a feast in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, like unto the feast that is in Judah” (1Ki 12:32) — a month he “had devised of his own heart” (1Ki 12:33). And Luke dates the Baptist's ministry to “the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar” (Luk 3:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fifteenth as the ordinal of fifteen; the fifth after the tenth.
webster_full: FIFTEENTH, a. The ordinal of fifteen; the fifth after the tenth.
corruption_summary: Jeroboam kept the right day in the wrong month, and every invented holy day since has copied his method.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeroboam's feast was careful. It fell on the fifteenth, like the LORD's; it had an altar, priests, and sacrifices, like the LORD's; and it was in the eighth month instead of the seventh, because he had devised the month of his own heart. First Kings 12:33 is the Bible's definition of will-worship: the outward form of what God commanded, on a calendar God did not give, for a reason the king found in himself. The corruption is not that men invent feasts — it is that they invent them to look like the ones God appointed, so that the worshipper cannot tell the fifteenth of the seventh from the fifteenth of the eighth. Luke 3:1 is the opposite use of a date: the gospel fixed in a Roman emperor's fifteenth year, so that no one could say it happened once upon a time.
roots_summary: Hebrew chamesh esreh (H2568, H6240), fifteen, fifteenth; Greek pentekaidekatos (G4003), fifteenth.
roots_lines: Hebrew chamesh esreh (H2568 with H6240) — fifteenth; Leviticus 23:6, 23:34, Numbers 33:3, 1 Kings 12:32–33.
usage: “The fifteenth day of this seventh month shall be the feast of tabernacles” — the LORD's calendar.
“In the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month… which he had devised of his own heart” — Jeroboam's.
“In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar” — the gospel dated.

pos: adj. (the ordinal of seventeen; rendering Hebrew sheva esreh)
etymology: Old English seofontēotha. The flood began and the ark came to rest on a seventeenth day, five months apart to the day.
biblical_def: “In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month, the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up” (Gen 7:11); “And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat” (Gen 8:4). Ahaziah began to reign over Israel “the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat” (1Ki 22:51), and Ahaz over Judah “in the seventeenth year of Pekah” (2Ki 16:1). The seventeenth lot of the priests fell to Hezir (1Ch 24:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines seventeenth as the ordinal of seventeen; the seventh after the tenth.
webster_full: SEVENTEENTH, a. The ordinal of seventeen; the seventh after the tenth.
corruption_summary: The flood is read as legend, and the record keeps a log by the day of the month.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 7 and 8 are written like a ship's log. The rain began on the seventeenth day of the second month; the waters prevailed a hundred and fifty days; the ark grounded on the seventeenth day of the seventh month — five months of thirty days, to the day. Legends do not keep dates, and the men who call the flood a myth have to explain why the myth has a calendar. The precision is the point: Moses is recording an event that happened to real people in a real year, and Peter builds a warning on it — the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished, and the heavens and the earth which are now are kept in store (2Pe 3:6–7). A judgment with a date is a judgment that can be believed in, and the next one has a day appointed too.
roots_lines: Hebrew sheva esreh (H7651 with H6240) — seventeenth; Genesis 7:11, 8:4, 1 Kings 22:51, 2 Kings 16:1, 1 Chronicles 24:15.
usage: “The seventeenth day of the month, the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up” — the flood dated.
“On the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat” — the ark grounded five months later, to the day.
“The seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat” — the reigns cross-dated.

pos: adj. (the ordinal of eighteen; rendering Hebrew shemoneh esreh)
etymology: Old English eahtatēotha. The eighteenth year of Josiah is the year the book was found and the passover kept.
biblical_def: “In the eighteenth year of king Josiah” the king sent Shaphan to the house of the LORD, and Hilkiah found the book of the law (2Ki 22:3); and the passover that followed had no equal since the judges, “in the eighteenth year of king Josiah, wherein this passover was holden to the LORD in Jerusalem” (2Ki 23:23; 2Ch 35:19). Abijam began to reign over Judah “in the eighteenth year of king Jeroboam” (1Ki 15:1), and Jehoram over Israel in “the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat” (2Ki 3:1). Jeremiah bought his field in the tenth year of Zedekiah, “which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar” (Jer 32:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eighteenth as the next in order after the seventeenth.
webster_full: EIGHTEENTH, a. The next in order after the seventeenth.
corruption_summary: Reformation is imagined as a mood that comes over a nation, and Josiah's came in a dated year, from a found book.
corruption_paragraphs: Josiah's reformation has a year, a workman, a book, and a passover, in that order. In his eighteenth year the temple was being repaired, the book of the law was found in the rubble of neglect, a scribe read it aloud, and a king rent his clothes. Everything after that — the covenant renewed, the idols ground to powder, the passover kept as none had been since the judges — came from the reading. The modern idea of revival is atmospheric; it is felt before it is founded. Second Kings 22 puts the Word first and the feeling second, and dates both, so that when men want to know what a reformation looks like they have a year to examine.
roots_lines: Hebrew shemoneh esreh (H8083 with H6240) — eighteenth; 2 Kings 22:3, 23:23, 2 Chronicles 34:8, 35:19, 1 Kings 15:1, Jeremiah 32:1.
usage: “In the eighteenth year of king Josiah” — the book found.
“Wherein this passover was holden to the LORD” — the same year, the feast kept.
“The eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar” — the siege counted from the other side.

pos: adj. (the ordinal of thirty; rendering Hebrew sheloshim)
etymology: Old English thrītigotha. Ezekiel's book opens in the thirtieth year, the age at which a priest would have begun his service.
biblical_def: “Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God” (Eze 1:1). Asa had “no more war unto the five and thirtieth year” of his reign (2Ch 15:19), and Baasha came up against Judah “in the six and thirtieth year” (2Ch 16:1). Jehoiachin was lifted out of prison “in the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity” (2Ki 25:27). Nehemiah went back to the king “in the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes” (Neh 13:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thirtieth as the ordinal of thirty; the tenth threefold.
webster_full: THIRTIETH, a. The ordinal of thirty; the tenth threefold.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel's thirtieth year is treated as a riddle, when it is the age of a priest whose first day of service came in exile, by a canal, with the temple far away.
corruption_paragraphs: The thirtieth year of Ezekiel 1:1 is the prophet's own age. Numbers 4:3 sets thirty as the year a son of Levi entered the service of the sanctuary, and Ezekiel was a priest (v. 3) who reached that year among the captives by the river of Chebar, five hundred miles from the altar he had trained for. Instead of the temple he was given the vision of the glory — the wheels, the living creatures, the likeness of a throne — and in the eleventh chapter he would watch that glory leave the temple he could not reach. The lesson is the one every displaced servant needs: the year of ordination came on schedule, and the LORD kept the appointment in the place where the man actually was.
roots_lines: Hebrew sheloshim (H7970) — thirty, thirtieth; Ezekiel 1:1, 2 Chronicles 15:19, 16:1, 2 Kings 25:27, Nehemiah 5:14, 13:6.
usage: “In the thirtieth year… the heavens were opened” — a priest's first year of service, kept in exile.
“No more war unto the five and thirtieth year” — Asa's long peace, and its end.
“In the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity” — Jehoiachin lifted up.
